body.heading: The body's memory
paragraphs: When your immune system defeats an infection, it keeps specialised memory cells that recognise that germ. Meet the same germ again and the response is faster and stronger — often so fast you never feel ill. A vaccine's job is to create that memory without the danger of the disease itself, using a weakened, inactivated or partial version of the germ, or instructions that let your own cells display a harmless piece of it.
It is less like medicine and more like a fire drill: a calm rehearsal today so that a real emergency is handled swiftly.

body.heading: Jenner and the milkmaids
paragraphs: Smallpox once killed or scarred a large share of everyone it infected. In 1796, the English doctor Edward Jenner tested a folk observation: milkmaids who had caught the mild disease cowpox seemed protected from smallpox. He showed that material from cowpox could indeed protect a person, and published his results for the world.

Jenner was building on older practices of deliberate mild exposure used in parts of Asia, Africa and the Ottoman world. His contribution was evidence, persistence and a name: vaccination, from vacca, the Latin word for cow. Louis Pasteur later extended the idea to other diseases, weakening germs in the laboratory to make new vaccines.

body.heading: The disease that no longer exists
paragraphs: In 1980, after a worldwide campaign of vaccination and surveillance, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated — the first disease deliberately wiped from the Earth, and still the only one to infect humans. Polio has since been pushed to the edge of eradication.
Vaccines remain one of the clearest demonstrations of an idea: that understanding how the body remembers can protect not just one person, but everyone they will ever meet.

takeaway: Vaccines rehearse the immune system safely, building memory without illness — an idea strong enough to erase smallpox from the world.
